hero.eyebrow: LittleLeap Studios · built by Mikael Dell’Anna
hero.title: I built a cartoon studio where AI agents do the work and I sign off the key steps
hero.lede: In eight weeks I went from one pilot episode to a studio that writes, draws, animates, voices, checks and publishes happy animal stories for children aged 3–7. I approve the story, new character looks and the final cut. Everything else runs on its own.

items.name: Model comparison
items.text: Playable Kie.ai and Quiver test clips with my decisions

ai.title: Every AI choice I made, and the tests behind it
ai.lede: I didn’t pick models on reputation. Each one earned its place in a side-by-side test, on my own characters, judged by measurable checks and by eye.

domains.title: Drawings
domains.story: I planned to draw locally with FLUX.2-klein on the Mac. For on-model characters I moved to Nano Banana Pro, editing one master drawing into ~30 poses per character.

tests.name: FLUX.2-klein-4B, local
tests.text: The pilot plan: free and private, but not consistent enough across poses

tests.name: Nano Banana Pro via OpenRouter
tests.text: Every pose an edit of one master drawing, so the cast stays on model. ~$0.14 an image

tests.name: Same model via Kie.ai
tests.text: Same quality and same failure modes, $0.09 an image. $0.12 vs $0.18 per usable drawing

tests.name: Own LoRAs on Qwen-Image-Edit
tests.text: Trained on RunPod for ~$15 as insurance if a closed model changes. 20 of 24 new poses on model

tests.name: AI edit vs code for the four-eyed Snail
tests.text: The AI fix kept 4 of 15 drawings clean; a small script fixed all 15 for $0

domains.title: Motion
domains.story: Smooth movement was the hardest part. I tried rigs, kits and puppets before landing on AI video between my own key drawings.

tests.name: Cut-up rigs and part kits
tests.text: Seams, floating parts, outlines that didn’t match

tests.name: Layered rig with mesh bending
tests.text: Pilot on Leo: the arm outlines never matched the body

tests.name: AI in-betweens, Seedance 2.0 fast
tests.text: First and last frame are my drawings; the model fills the motion. “Exactly how it should be done”

tests.name: Wan 3.0
tests.text: Passed 3 of 3 clips at $0.32, against ~$0.50 for Seedance fast on Kie

tests.name: Seedance 2.0 mini
tests.text: Missed the last key and drifted grey: 0 of 3

tests.name: PixVerse v6 transition
tests.text: Ignored the locked camera and zoomed in: 0 of 3

tests.name: QuiverAI SVG animation
tests.text: Fine for props and idle loops, but puppet-style for characters

domains.title: Voices
domains.story: Each character has one voice, cloned into five more languages so a child hears the same friend in Spanish or German.

tests.name: Orpheus TTS 3B
tests.text: The pilot plan; replaced by voices with more control per character

tests.name: Kokoro
tests.text: Clean English voices with per-character speed and pitch

tests.name: Chatterbox expressive
tests.text: From EP06, more acting in English lines, cloned from each Kokoro voice

tests.name: Chatterbox Multilingual for dubs
tests.text: MIT licence, runs locally, voice match 0.63

tests.name: OmniVoice
tests.text: Clearer, but the model weights are licensed for non-commercial use only

tests.name: Whisper and speaker checks
tests.text: Whisper hears only the scripted words; a speaker model scores voice match

domains.title: Music
domains.story: I started with beds synthesised in code, then remixed them in Suno through seven versions into my first album.

tests.name: Own synthesised beds
tests.text: Code-made cues with no licence questions, still the melodic source

tests.name: Suno v1–v3: storybook and music box
tests.text: Too Japanese, not classical enough

tests.name: Suno v4–v5: piano and orchestra
tests.text: Beautiful, but swells and climaxes fought the voices

tests.name: Suno v6–v7: scene-fitted underscore
tests.text: Briefed per real scene use; best take picked by measured endings and steadiness

tests.name: 432 Hz retune and album
tests.text: Measured each track’s tuning and resampled it; released as MKDA on 28 stores

standing.title: The channel over time, and what moved it
standing.lede: Updated automatically. Each flag is something I changed; the verdict says what the numbers did after.
standing.insightBefore: YouTube already shows my episodes about 600 times a day.
standing.insightMark: The click and the first 15 seconds
standing.insightNote: So from EP07 I’m changing the packaging, not the volume: one big face with one clear feeling on the thumbnail, story-first titles, and a character talking to the child from frame 0.

learnings.title: What I learned

films.name: Turn every note into a rule
films.text: My notes fell into nine repeat categories. Repeating one is now a blocker

films.name: More process isn’t more quality
films.text: EP06 hit 84 versions and $31 under a heavier process; I went back to the October gates

films.name: Design props for the action
films.text: The mitten’s opening was too small to climb in. One late prop cost about 20 versions

films.name: Machines check before I do
films.text: Automatic staging checks took EP02 from 173 issues to zero before I watched

films.name: Whole drawings beat rigs
films.text: Every shortcut failed; pose libraries plus AI in-betweens hold

films.name: Pay per usable result
films.text: AI services bill wrong outputs too. I compare models on price divided by pass rate

audience: Packaging beats distribution: impressions came, clicks didn’t
Made for Kids removes A/B tests, end screens, comments and cards
Dubs bring ~5% of views; Shorts are barely shown
Kids ads pay about $0.33 per 1,000 views, so ~3M views per $1,000
Each episode must be clearly different under YouTube’s inauthentic-content policy
operations: One Mac mini is a single point of failure
Empty prepaid credit silently stops jobs
Browser automation needs workarounds, like 10 MB upload chunks
Rules kept in two places drift apart
I’m the bottleneck, so the agents now use defaults and a best-result rule
